The thinking

The claim, kept in view

From scattered channel reports to one weekly decision a small team could actually make.

28 sample days
$40,152
3 markets
US · UK · DE
revenue ÷ spend
4.56×

The argument scrolls; the claim and its measured context stay beside it.

Figures: synthetic sample dataset, all markets, ending Sep 28, 2026. ROAS from the same period as the dashboard.

Every channel told a different story. The useful question was not “which chart looks best?”, but “where is the next constraint, and what evidence would change our mind?”

1Give every number a context

Market and time controls update the whole report together. Spend, attributed revenue and orders share a visible period; ROAS is revenue divided by spend.

2Keep forecasts separate from observations

The budget slider produces an illustrative scenario using a stated constant-ROAS assumption. It never changes the historical dataset or pretends to predict reality.

3Let people inspect the details

An accessible chart summary, the product summary table and daily CSV export make the sample report inspectable. A dashboard is useful when its summary can be traced back.

Outcome

What it produced

The dashboard opens on the question the team kept circling: where is the next constraint. Four weeks of sample spend, every daily row behind the chart, and the CSV export carries the same numbers the chart is drawn from.

AI PRODUCT DESIGN · 2025–2026

Less blank-page time, more useful direction

A product concept for small commerce teams who need a shared starting point before they write, shoot and publish content.

The question

Role in this fictional case

How this prototype works

A deterministic local template maps your audience, product detail, tone and length into a storyboard. The same inputs produce the same draft. It does not infer product facts, generate images or measure likely performance.

Shot list
  1. 0–3s

    Open on a familiar everyday moment for “Commuters who carry a reusable bottle”. Keep the Ceramic bottle in the frame.

    On-screen text: Make a little room for the Ceramic bottle.
  2. 3–10s

Call to action

Take a closer look at the Ceramic bottle.

Why this structure

The calm tone shapes the opening. The audience (Commuters who carry a reusable bottle) sets the first scene, while “a ceramic body and screw-top lid” gives the middle scene a specific detail to show. This is a local template draft, with no external AI service; verify product facts before publishing.

The interactive prototype needs JavaScript, and this browser has it switched off, so its controls are taken out of the page rather than left here answering nothing. The written case, its tables and every figure behind them need no script.

The thinking

The initial concept asked for too much and gave too little guidance. A useful brief needs a product, a person and a purpose — not a wall of empty fields.

1Make the first step concrete

Start with a usable example and a small set of meaningful inputs. People can see the kind of answer the workflow is designed to produce.

2Keep the reasoning beside the output

A hook, shot list and call to action are paired with a rationale. The team can discuss why a direction fits instead of accepting polished text uncritically.

3Be honest about the prototype

The demo transforms the inputs with local templates. It does not call an AI model. A production model would need quality evaluation, editing, recovery and cost controls.

Outcome

What it produced

Product, audience, one verifiable detail, tone and length become a shootable brief in the browser, and the downloaded file is the same text the screen shows.

RESEARCH & PRODUCT STRATEGY · 2026

Build the right small thing first

An illustrative research exercise about helping small commerce teams turn weekly learning into their next product decision.

Fictional portfolioILLUSTRATIVE CASE STUDY
In this caseSix sample notesConceptThe thinkingWhat it produced

PROJECT SNAPSHOT

The question

What would we build first if we cared about learning speed as much as feature count?

Role in this fictional case

Research planning, synthesis, concept comparison and MVP scope.

Research
6 fictional interviews
Exploration
3 concepts
Decision
1 focused MVP

Notice → Interpret → Choose

  1. 1

    Notice

    Scattered reports. Repeated questions.

  2. 2

    Interpret

    No shared starting point for a decision.

  3. 3

    Choose

    A brief the team can discuss.

Six sample notes

One interview, one note. Read side by side, the same question arrives from different roles, which is why the team needed a shared starting point before it needed another report.

Six invented interviews, one note per role — recurring question, workaround, consequence.
InterviewRecurring questionWorkaround todayConsequence
Merchandiser · three marketsWhich number do I trust this week?Rebuilds one sheet from three exports every MondayThe first hour of the week goes to reconciliation instead of a decision
Founder · two-person storeDid the campaign actually work?Screenshots the ad dashboard into a slideThe team debates the story, not the next test
Operations lead · seasonal catalogueWhy did orders dip?Asks the warehouse and the channel owner separatelyTwo answers arrive, with no shared starting point
Marketing manager · six channelsIs this a channel problem or a product problem?Combines channel reports by hand at month endLearning arrives after the decision it should have informed
Agency strategist · five clientsWhat did we learn last month?Keeps a running document nobody reopensEvery kickoff restarts from memory
Founder · after a failed launchWhat would change our mind?Asks for more dataFeatures keep shipping without naming the behaviour to watch

Six invented interviews. The quotes are illustrative composites, not transcripts; the notes demonstrate the synthesis method rather than real research evidence.

Compare three concepts

A long feature list made the opportunity feel bigger but the first useful release harder to see. The table is the whole comparison — the buttons only move emphasis.

Three concepts, compared on effort, value and learning speed — invented material for teaching.
ConceptEffortValue nowLearning speedNext test
Decision briefLowHigh, immediatelyFast — one shared artifactDoes a weekly brief help the team pick one action?
Report hubMediumMediumSlow — dashboards answer old questionsWhich report actually changes a decision?
Automation suiteHighUnvalidatedSlow — dependencies before learningCan a small prototype survive failed inputs and handover?

Invented research and an illustrative comparison demonstrate the decision process, not real interviews or commercial validation.

The thinking

A long feature list made the opportunity feel bigger, but made the first useful release harder to see. The research needed to lead to a choice.

1Group by the decision people need to make

Sample notes are organised around recurring questions, workarounds and consequences. Every finding is labelled illustrative, not presented as real interview evidence.

2Make trade-offs explicit

Compare a report hub, a decision brief and a full automation suite using effort, value and learning speed. The chosen concept keeps the first release small and inspectable.

3Choose the next test before the next feature

A next-step plan names the behaviour to observe and what would change the direction. No fabricated success percentage is needed to explain a defensible choice.

Outcome

What it produced

Six sample interviews and three compared concepts resolve into one focused MVP, and the behaviour to observe next is named before the next feature is written.
